steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Sampling: random (equal chance, unbiased but hard), systematic (every nth, simple but may bias), stratified (proportional, representative but complex), opportunity (available, quick but biased), volunteer (self-selected, motivated but unrepresentative).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Reliability: consistency - repeat study, same results. Improved by: standardised procedures, clear operationalisation. Validity: accuracy - measures what it claims. Improved by: ecological validity, triangulation.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Operationalisation: defining concepts precisely so they can be measured. Example: 'social class' must be operationalised as specific categories. Good operationalisation improves both reliability and validity.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Ethical principles (BSA): informed consent, confidentiality, right to withdraw, protection from harm, avoidance of deception, sensitivity to participants' values and culture.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe different sampling methods and evaluate when each would be most appropriate. | Explain the difference between reliability and validity. | A sociologist wants to study domestic violence. Evaluate the ethical issues.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Sampling: random (unbiased, hard) vs opportunity (easy, biased). Reliability = CONSISTENCY. Validity = ACCURACY. Both needed. BSA Ethics: consent + confidentiality + protection + withdrawal + avoid deception + debrief.
